subject: Chemistry
title: Priya's Chemistry Lab: Understanding the Mole
hook: Why do chemists count atoms in moles? A 11th grader's journey into chemistry's most powerful counting tool.

slides.title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
slides.storyContext: Priya enters the chemistry lab at Delhi Public School, ready to understand how chemists work with invisible atoms and molecules.

image.alt: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: The Mole Mystery
slides.storyContext: Priya asks Mr. Sharma: 'Sir, atoms are SO tiny—how do you even count them when mixing chemicals?' Mr. Sharma smiles and says, 'That's exactly why we invented the mole. Watch.'

image.alt: The Mole Mystery — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: What is the Mole?

points.label: Definition
points.text: 1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons)

points.label: Avogadro's Number
points.text: Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹

points.label: Why this number?
points.text: Carbon-12 has exactly 12 atomic mass units (amu); 1 mole of ¹²C has mass = 12 g

example.problem: How many atoms are in 1 mole of oxygen?
example.solution: 1 mole of O contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms (by definition of Avogadro's number).

slides.inSimpleWords: A mole is a counting unit for chemists. Just like a dozen = 12, a mole = 6.022 × 10²³. Chemists use it because atoms are incredibly small and too many to count individually.

image.alt: What is the Mole? — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: Molar Mass & Molecular Weight

points.label: Molar Mass
points.text: Mass of 1 mole of a substance in grams (numerically = molecular weight in amu)

points.label: Example: Water (H₂O)
points.text: H = 1, O = 16 → molecular weight = 1×2 + 16 = 18 amu → molar mass = 18 g/mol

points.label: Calculation rule
points.text: Molar mass (g/mol) = sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the formula

example.problem: Find molar mass of NaCl (Na=23, Cl=35.5)

slides.inSimpleWords: Molar mass is the weight of 1 mole of a substance in grams. It's easy to calculate: just add up all the atomic masses in the formula.

image.alt: Molar Mass & Molecular Weight — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: Moles from Mass & Volume

points.label: From mass
points.text: Number of moles = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol)

points.label: From volume (gases at STP)
points.text: 1 mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 L (molar volume)

points.label: STP definition
points.text: Standard Temperature (0°C) and Pressure (1 atm)

example.problem: How many moles in 36 g of water (M=18)?
example.solution: Moles = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 moles

slides.inSimpleWords: You can find moles by dividing mass by molar mass. For gases, remember that 1 mole = 22.4 L at STP—a handy memory tool!

image.alt: Moles from Mass & Volume — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: Empirical & Molecular Formulas

points.label: Empirical formula
points.text: Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms (e.g., CH for benzene)

points.label: Molecular formula
points.text: Actual number of atoms in one molecule (e.g., C₆H₆ for benzene)

points.label: Relationship
points.text: Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ, where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical mass

example.problem: Empirical formula CH₂O, empirical mass 30. If molecular mass = 180, find molecular formula.
example.solution: n = 180 ÷ 30 = 6. Molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose)

slides.inSimpleWords: Empirical formula is the simplest ratio; molecular formula shows the real molecule. Glucose looks simple as CH₂O but is actually C₆H₁₂O₆.

image.alt: Empirical & Molecular Formulas — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: Limiting Reagent (Indian Kitchen Example)

points.label: Definition
points.text: The reactant that runs out first, controlling how much product can form

points.label: Example: Making dosa
points.text: Recipe: 1 cup rice flour + 1 cup lentil flour → 4 dosas. If you have 3 cups rice but only 1 cup lentils, lentils limit you to 4 dosas.

points.label: Calculation
points.text: Convert all reactants to moles. Divide by stoichiometric coefficients. The smallest result is the limiting reagent.

example.problem: React 10 g Fe + 10 g Cl₂. M(Fe)=56, M(Cl₂)=71. Which is limiting? (Reaction: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃)
example.solution: Fe: 10÷56 = 0.179 mol. Cl₂: 10÷71 = 0.141 mol. Cl₂ has fewer relative moles → Cl₂ is limiting.

slides.inSimpleWords: In any reaction, one ingredient always runs out first—that's the limiting reagent. It's like making dosa: if you have lots of rice but little lentil flour, the lentil flour stops you.

image.alt: Limiting Reagent (Indian Kitchen Example) — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: Worked Problem: Stoichiometry Calculation
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma gives the class a real lab problem. Priya solves it step by step.

example.problem: Calcium reacts with oxygen: 2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO. If 4 g of Ca burns, how many grams of CaO form? (M(Ca)=40, M(CaO)=56)
example.solution: Step 1: Moles of Ca = 4 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mol. Step 2: From stoichiometry, 2 mol Ca → 2 mol CaO, so 0.1 mol Ca → 0.1 mol CaO. Step 3: Mass of CaO = 0.1 × 56 = 5.6 g.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert grams to moles, use the balanced equation to find product moles, then convert back to grams. This is the heart of stoichiometry.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Stoichiometry Calculation — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: Your Turn: Calculate Moles
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma challenges Priya and Arjun: 'How many moles of NaOH are in a 500 mL solution of 2 M concentration?'

example.problem: A solution has molarity M = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution. If 2 M NaOH, 500 mL = 0.5 L, find moles.
example.solution: Moles = Molarity × Volume (L) = 2 × 0.5 = 1 mole of NaOH.

image.alt: Your Turn: Calculate Moles — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

slides.title: Key Takeaways

points.text: 1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number)
Molar mass (g/mol) = sum of atomic masses in the formula
Moles = mass ÷ molar mass
1 mole of gas at STP = 22.4 L
Limiting reagent controls product amount
Empirical formula is simplest ratio; molecular formula is the actual molecule

slides.inSimpleWords: Chemistry is about counting particles in moles, relating mass and moles through molar mass, and using stoichiometry to predict reaction amounts.

image.alt: Key Takeaways — Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

subject: Chemistry
title: Inside the Atom: Priya's Quantum Journey
hook: From plum pudding to electron orbitals—discover how scientists unveiled the hidden architecture of the atom.

slides.title: Structure of Atom
slides.storyContext: Priya attends her first advanced chemistry class. Dr. Das begins: 'Everything you see—your phone, your food, even you—is made of atoms. But what's inside?'

image.alt: Structure of Atom — Structure of Atom

slides.title: The Quest to Understand Atoms
slides.storyContext: Dr. Das explains that over 200 years, scientists discovered layer by layer what atoms are made of. From Thomson's electron to Rutherford's nucleus to Bohr's model—each breakthrough rewrote the picture.

image.alt: The Quest to Understand Atoms — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Subatomic Particles

points.label: Proton (p⁺)
points.text: Positive charge, mass ≈ 1 amu, found in nucleus

points.label: Neutron (n⁰)
points.text: Neutral (no charge), mass ≈ 1 amu, found in nucleus

points.label: Electron (e⁻)
points.text: Negative charge, mass ≈ 1/1836 amu, found in orbitals around nucleus

example.problem: Oxygen has 8 protons and 8 neutrons. How many electrons in a neutral O atom?
example.solution: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons. So O has 8 electrons. Mass number A = 8 + 8 = 16 (written ¹⁶O).

slides.inSimpleWords: Atoms have three building blocks: protons (positive, heavy, in center), neutrons (neutral, heavy, in center), and electrons (negative, light, spinning around the center).

image.alt: Subatomic Particles — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Atomic Number & Mass Number

points.label: Atomic Number (Z)
points.text: Number of protons in nucleus = defines the element

points.label: Mass Number (A)
points.text: Total protons + neutrons (A = Z + N)

points.label: Isotopes
points.text: Same element (same Z), different neutrons (different A). Example: ¹²C and ¹⁴C are isotopes of carbon.

example.problem: Write the atomic structure of ¹⁹F (Fluorine). M(F)=19.
example.solution: Z = 9 (atomic number of F), A = 19, so N = 19 - 9 = 10. Fluorine has 9 protons, 10 neutrons, 9 electrons.

slides.inSimpleWords: Atomic number tells you which element it is (defines identity). Mass number is protons + neutrons (almost all the mass).

image.alt: Atomic Number & Mass Number — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Bohr's Model of Hydrogen

points.label: Bohr's postulates
points.text: Electrons orbit in fixed energy levels (n = 1, 2, 3, ...). Each level has maximum electrons = 2n².

points.label: Energy levels
points.text: n=1 (K shell): 2 e⁻ max; n=2 (L shell): 8 e⁻ max; n=3 (M shell): 18 e⁻ max

points.label: Radiation rule
points.text: When electron jumps down, it emits light (energy). Hydrogen spectrum shows specific lines (Lyman, Balmer, etc.).

example.problem: An electron in hydrogen jumps from n=3 to n=1. Does it emit or absorb energy?
example.solution: n=3 is higher energy than n=1. The electron loses energy and emits light (radiation).

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons don't fall into the nucleus because they orbit in shells. When an electron drops to a lower shell, it releases light—this is how hydrogen lamps glow.

image.alt: Bohr's Model of Hydrogen — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Quantum Mechanical Model & Orbitals

points.label: Orbital
points.text: Region of space where electron is likely to be found (not a fixed path like Bohr's orbit)

points.label: Quantum numbers
points.text: n (principal, 1-7), l (angular momentum, 0 to n-1), m (magnetic, -l to +l), s (spin, ±½)

points.label: Orbital shapes
points.text: s orbitals (spherical), p orbitals (dumbbell), d orbitals (cloverleaf), f orbitals (complex)

example.problem: How many orbitals in the 2p subshell?
example.solution: For n=2, l=1 (p), m can be -1, 0, +1. So 3 p orbitals. Each can hold 2 electrons (spin up/down), total capacity = 6 electrons in 2p.

slides.inSimpleWords: Modern chemistry doesn't picture electrons as orbiting like planets. Instead, they exist as 'clouds' of probability around the nucleus—orbitals.

image.alt: Quantum Mechanical Model & Orbitals — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Aufbau Principle & Electron Configuration

points.label: Aufbau Principle
points.text: Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, ...

points.label: Pauli Exclusion
points.text: No two electrons can have the same four quantum numbers (max 2 per orbital)

points.label: Hund's Rule
points.text: Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first (parallel spins), then pair up.

example.problem: Write electron configuration of Oxygen (Z=8).
example.solution: O (8 e⁻): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. Or abbreviated: [He] 2s² 2p⁴.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons fill orbitals like students filling seats in a movie hall—lowest energy rows first, then spread out before doubling up.

image.alt: Aufbau Principle & Electron Configuration — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Periodic Trends from Electron Configuration

points.label: Valence electrons
points.text: Outermost shell electrons—determine chemical behavior

points.label: Period
points.text: Horizontal row of periodic table = number of electron shells

points.label: Group
points.text: Vertical column = number of valence electrons (for main group)

example.problem: Silicon (Si, Z=14) config: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p². Which period and group?
example.solution: Highest n=3 → Period 3. Valence e⁻ = 2+2=4 → Group 14. Si forms 4 bonds.

slides.inSimpleWords: The periodic table is just a filing system for electron configurations. Elements in the same column have similar chemistry because they have the same number of valence electrons.

image.alt: Periodic Trends from Electron Configuration — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Worked Problem: Hydrogen Spectrum
slides.storyContext: Dr. Das shows the class a beautiful spectrum from a hydrogen lamp and asks: 'Why do we see these specific colors, not a rainbow?'

example.problem: The Balmer series (n=2 ← n) shows visible lines. If an electron drops from n=4 to n=2, is this visible light? (Balmer covers n ≥ 3 → n=2)
example.solution: Yes. This is Hγ (green line, 486 nm). The electron loses energy equal to E = E₄ - E₂, which is in the visible range. Each line corresponds to a different starting level (n=3, 4, 5, ...).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrogen emits light only at specific wavelengths because electrons can only occupy certain energy levels. Each color represents a specific electron jump.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Hydrogen Spectrum — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Your Turn: Electron Configuration
slides.storyContext: Priya is given a surprise quiz. 'Write the electron configuration of Sulfur (Z=16) and identify how many unpaired electrons it has.'

example.problem: S (16 e⁻): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. In 3p, how many unpaired e⁻?
example.solution: 3p⁴ means 4 electrons in 3 p-orbitals (3 total). By Hund's rule: ↑ ↑ ↑ (first), then ↑↓ in one, so 2 unpaired. (Or arranged as ↑ ↑↓ ↑)—2 unpaired.

image.alt: Your Turn: Electron Configuration — Structure of Atom

slides.title: Atomic Structure Summary

points.text: Atoms = nucleus (protons + neutrons) + electrons in orbitals
Z = atomic number (protons), A = mass number (protons + neutrons)
Bohr model: electrons in fixed shells; Quantum model: electrons in orbitals (probability regions)
Aufbau, Pauli, Hund: rules for electron configuration
Valence electrons determine chemistry
Periodic table reflects electron configuration patterns

slides.inSimpleWords: The atom has a tiny, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons in layers and orbitals. The arrangement of electrons explains why chemistry works the way it does.

image.alt: Atomic Structure Summary — Structure of Atom

subject: Chemistry
chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
title: The Periodic Table: Nature's Masterpiece
hook: Why do alkali metals explode in water and noble gases never react? The periodic table holds the secret.

slides.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
slides.storyContext: Dr. Gupta asks the class: 'Look around. You see salt, water, air, metals, plastics. How is everything organized at the atomic level?'

image.alt: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Mendeleev's Gamble
slides.storyContext: In 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev arranged 63 known elements by atomic weight and boldly predicted missing elements. When gallium was discovered exactly where he predicted, science changed forever. The periodic table was born.

image.alt: Mendeleev's Gamble — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Modern Periodic Table Structure

points.label: Periods
points.text: Horizontal rows (1-7). Period number = number of electron shells.

points.label: Groups
points.text: Vertical columns (1-18). Group = number of valence electrons (for main group)

points.label: Blocks
points.text: s-block (Groups 1-2), p-block (Groups 13-18), d-block (Groups 3-12), f-block (below table)

example.problem: Where is Phosphorus (P, Z=15) on the periodic table?
example.solution: Config: [Ne] 3s² 3p³. Period = 3 (3 shells), Group = 15 (5 valence e⁻). P is Period 3, Group 15, p-block.

slides.inSimpleWords: The periodic table is organized into rows (periods) and columns (groups). Higher period = more electron shells. Elements in the same group behave similarly.

image.alt: Modern Periodic Table Structure — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Periodic Trends: Atomic Radius

points.label: Across a period (left to right)
points.text: Atomic radius DECREASES. Reason: more protons, same shell → stronger pull on electrons.

points.label: Down a group
points.text: Atomic radius INCREASES. Reason: new electron shell added with each period.

points.label: Example
points.text: Na (186 pm) > Mg (160 pm) > Al (143 pm) across Period 3. But Na > K (227 pm) down Group 1.

example.problem: Compare atomic radii: Na vs Cl vs K
example.solution: Same period: Na > Cl (Cl is smaller, more protons pull electrons in). Same group: Na < K (K has extra shell). Order: Cl < Na < K.

slides.inSimpleWords: Atoms get smaller as you go right across a row (more protons pulling in), but bigger going down a column (new shells added).

image.alt: Periodic Trends: Atomic Radius — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Ionization Enthalpy (Ionization Energy)

points.label: Definition
points.text: Energy needed to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻

points.label: Trend across period
points.text: INCREASES (smaller atoms, harder to remove e⁻)

points.label: Trend down group
points.text: DECREASES (larger atoms, easier to remove outer e⁻)

example.problem: Why is Na's first ionization energy (496 kJ/mol) lower than Mg's (738 kJ/mol)?
example.solution: Na has one 3s electron; Mg has two 3s electrons. Mg's full s-orbital is more stable. Also, Mg is smaller (more nuclear pull), but the filled-orbital stability dominates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Loosely-held outer electrons (like in alkali metals) have low ionization energy—they're easy to remove. Tightly-held electrons (noble gases, small atoms) have high ionization energy.

image.alt: Ionization Enthalpy (Ionization Energy) — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Electronegativity

points.label: Definition
points.text: Ability of an atom to attract electrons in a covalent bond (Pauling scale, 0.79-3.98)

points.label: Trend
points.text: INCREASES across period (left to right), DECREASES down group

points.label: Most electronegative
points.text: Fluorine (3.98). Least: Francium (0.79).

example.problem: In H-Cl bond, which atom pulls electrons more? (H=2.1, Cl=3.0)
example.solution: Cl (3.0) > H (2.1), so Cl is more electronegative. Electrons shift toward Cl, making it partially negative (δ⁻) and H partially positive (δ⁺).

slides.inSimpleWords: Electronegativity measures an atom's 'greediness' for electrons. Fluorine is the greediest; alkali metals are the most generous.

image.alt: Electronegativity — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Electron Affinity

points.label: Definition
points.text: Energy released when 1 mole of electrons added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g)

points.label: Trend
points.text: Generally INCREASES across period (more negative/larger release)

points.label: Exception
points.text: Halogens have highest (F, Cl, Br release most energy when gaining e⁻). Noble gases have near-zero (already stable).

example.problem: Cl gains 1 electron readily (EA = -349 kJ/mol, negative = energy released). Why doesn't Cl⁻ gain another?
example.solution: Cl⁻ is negatively charged; repelling another electron requires energy input, not release. Second electron affinity is positive (unfavorable).

slides.inSimpleWords: Atoms that are 'hungry' for electrons (like halogens, especially Cl and F) have large negative electron affinities. They release lots of energy when filling their valence shell.

image.alt: Electron Affinity — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Metallic Character & Block Classification

points.label: Metallic character
points.text: Ability to lose electrons / form cations. DECREASES across period, INCREASES down group.

points.label: Metals
points.text: Left side of table (s, d, f blocks). Conduct electricity, malleable, shiny.

points.label: Nonmetals
points.text: Right side (most of p-block). Poor conductors, brittle, dull.

points.label: Metalloids
points.text: Boundary: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te. Semiconductors.

example.problem: Which is more metallic: Na or Al?
example.solution: Same period (3), Na is left of Al → Na is more metallic. Na forms Na⁺ easily; Al forms Al³⁺.

slides.inSimpleWords: The left side of the periodic table is metals (elements that give electrons). The right side is nonmetals (elements that take electrons). Metalloids are the border.

image.alt: Metallic Character & Block Classification — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: p, d, f Block Elements

points.label: p-block
points.text: Main-group elements (Groups 13-18). Boron to noble gases. Includes metals, metalloids, nonmetals.

points.label: d-block (transition metals)
points.text: Groups 3-12. Variable oxidation states, colored compounds, magnetic properties. Iron, copper, zinc.

points.label: f-block (lanthanides & actinides)
points.text: Rare earths. Fill f-orbitals. Lanthanides: La-Lu (70-71). Actinides: Ac-Lr (89-103).

example.problem: Why are transition metals like Fe, Cu colored in solution while main-group metals like NaCl are colorless?
example.solution: d-block metals have unfilled d-orbitals. Electrons jump between d-orbitals easily, absorbing visible light (colored). Main-group cations (Na⁺) have full shells; no easy transitions, no color.

slides.inSimpleWords: Transition metals (middle of the table) have unique properties: colors, variable charges, magnetic behavior. This is because their d-orbitals are being filled.

image.alt: p, d, f Block Elements — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Worked Problem: Periodic Trends Comparison
slides.storyContext: Dr. Gupta assigns a comparison problem. Priya tackles it systematically.

example.problem: Compare Cl, S, and Si in terms of: (a) atomic radius, (b) ionization energy, (c) electronegativity.
example.solution: (a) Atomic radius: Si > S > Cl (Si has 3 shells, S & Cl have 3 shells, but S left of Cl). Actual: Si (118 pm) > S (104 pm) > Cl (99 pm). (b) Ionization Energy: Cl > S > Si (harder to remove e⁻ from smaller, less metallic atoms). (c) Electronegativity: Cl (3.0) > S (2.5) > Si (1.9).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the two rules: across a period, trends go one way; down a group, the opposite. Memorize the directions, and you can compare any two elements.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Periodic Trends Comparison — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Why Do Alkali Metals Explode in Water?
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Dr. Gupta, why does sodium explode in water, but magnesium just burns, and calcium reacts calmly?' Dr. Gupta smiles: 'It's all in the periodic table.'

example.problem: Na reacts explosively: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑. Mg reacts more slowly: Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂↑. Explain.
example.solution: Na has very low ionization energy (496 kJ/mol)—it gives electrons very easily. The reaction releases SO much energy that the hydrogen gas ignites and explodes. Mg (738 kJ/mol) is harder to ionize, so slower, cooler reaction.

image.alt: Why Do Alkali Metals Explode in Water? — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

slides.title: Periodic Table Mastery

points.text: Period number = shells; Group (main group) = valence electrons
Atomic radius: increases down, decreases across
Ionization energy: increases across, decreases down
Electronegativity: increases across, decreases down
Metallic character: increases down, decreases across
d-block (transition metals) and f-block (rare earths) have unique properties from partially filled inner orbitals

slides.inSimpleWords: The periodic table is a map of chemistry. Learn the trends, and you can predict how any element will behave—without memorizing everything.

image.alt: Periodic Table Mastery — Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

subject: Chemistry
title: How Atoms Hold Hands: Bonding & Shapes
hook: Why does water form a V-shape? Why is ice less dense than liquid water? The answer lies in how atoms bond.

slides.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel holds up two beakers: one with salt (ionic), one with sugar (covalent). 'Same carbon atoms inside both, yet one dissolves instantly, the other resists. Why?'

image.alt: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Why Do Atoms Bond?
slides.storyContext: Atoms bond to achieve lower energy. Most stable configuration: filled valence shells (octet rule). Atoms will give, take, or share electrons to reach this stability. Different strategies = different bond types.

image.alt: Why Do Atoms Bond? — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Ionic Bonding: Complete Electron Transfer

points.label: Definition
points.text: Metal GIVES electrons to nonmetal. Electrostatic attraction between cation and anion.

points.label: Example: NaCl
points.text: Na (1 valence e⁻) → gives to Cl (7 valence e⁻). Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract strongly.

points.label: Properties
points.text: Crystalline solids, high melting point, conduct in molten state or aqueous solution, brittle.

example.problem: Write the electron transfer for MgO formation.
example.solution: Mg (2 e⁻) → transfers both to O (6 e⁻). Mg²⁺ + O²⁻ → MgO. Both now have stable octets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ionic bonds form when one atom completely gives electrons to another, creating charged ions that attract each other—like a magnet.

image.alt: Ionic Bonding: Complete Electron Transfer — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing

points.label: Definition
points.text: Atoms SHARE electrons in orbitals. Both atoms benefit from the shared pair.

points.label: Single, double, triple bonds
points.text: C-H: 1 pair (single), O=O: 2 pairs (double), N≡N: 3 pairs (triple).

points.label: Polar vs. nonpolar
points.text: Nonpolar: equal sharing (Cl-Cl, C-C). Polar: unequal sharing (H-Cl, C-O)—atom with higher electronegativity pulls more.

example.problem: Draw Lewis structure of CO₂. Are there any lone pairs?
example.solution: C is central (less electronegative), O atoms on either side. O=C=O. C has NO lone pairs (4 bonds). Each O has 2 lone pairs (total 4 electrons not bonding).

slides.inSimpleWords: Covalent bonds are atoms sharing electrons to fill their shells. Shared electrons spend more time near the more electronegative atom (polar).

image.alt: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Lewis Structures & Formal Charge

points.label: Octet rule
points.text: Atoms aim for 8 valence electrons (except H: 2)

points.label: Formal charge
points.text: FC = valence e⁻ - (lone pairs + ½ bonding e⁻). Minimize formal charges.

points.label: Example: Sulfur in H₂SO₄
points.text: S can expand octet (d-orbitals available), holding up to 12 e⁻ (6 bonds).

example.problem: Draw resonance structures for NO₃⁻ (nitrate ion).
example.solution: N is central (5 e⁻ + 1 from charge = 6). Forms 3 bonds with O atoms. One N=O (double), two N-O (single) with negative on the single-bonded O. Three resonance forms: the double bond rotates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lewis structures show where electrons are. Formal charge helps us pick the most realistic structure when multiple arrangements are possible.

image.alt: Lewis Structures & Formal Charge — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Valence Bond Theory & Hybridization

points.label: Overlap
points.text: Bonds form when atomic orbitals overlap. More overlap = stronger bond.

points.label: Hybridization
points.text: Mixing of orbitals to match molecular geometry. sp (linear), sp² (trigonal), sp³ (tetrahedral).

points.label: Example: Methane CH₄
points.text: C: 1s² 2s² 2p². Hybridizes to sp³ (4 equal orbitals), forming 4 identical C-H bonds at 109.5° angles.

example.problem: Ethene (C₂H₄): What is the hybridization of each carbon?
example.solution: Each C forms 3 bonds (2 C-H + 1 C=C). sp² hybridization. The C=C is σ + π bond. Bond angle ≈ 120°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Atoms can reshape their orbitals (hybridize) to match the shape of the molecule they're forming. This explains why bonds are arranged the way they are.

image.alt: Valence Bond Theory & Hybridization — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Molecular Shape

points.label: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion)
points.text: Electron pairs (bonding + lone) repel each other. They arrange to maximize distance.

points.label: Geometry from electron pairs
points.text: 2 pairs: linear. 3: trigonal planar. 4: tetrahedral. 5: trigonal bipyramidal. 6: octahedral.

points.label: Molecular shape
points.text: Ignore lone pairs for the final shape name, but they affect bond angles.

example.problem: What is the shape of NH₃ (ammonia)?
example.solution: N (5 e⁻) + 3 H (1 e⁻ each) = 8 e⁻ total = 4 electron pairs. One lone pair on N. Electron geometry: tetrahedral. Molecular shape: trigonal pyramidal (pyramid, not flat). Bond angle < 109.5° due to lone-pair repulsion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electron pairs push away from each other, spreading out as far as possible. This decides the shape of the molecule—V-shaped water, tetrahedral methane, etc.

image.alt: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Molecular Shape — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Hydrogen Bonding & Intermolecular Forces

points.label: Hydrogen bond
points.text: Special case of polar covalent bonding. H bonded to F, O, or N acts as partial positive; lone pair on F/O/N is attracted.

points.label: Strength order
points.text: Ionic > Hydrogen bond > Dipole-dipole > London forces (weakest)

points.label: Example: Water
points.text: H-O-H. Partial positive H on one molecule attracts lone pair on O of another. Creates hydrogen-bonded network—explains high boiling point (100°C vs NH₃ at -33°C).

example.problem: Why does ice float? (Hint: Hydrogen bonding in solid water.)
example.solution: In ice, hydrogen bonds form a crystalline lattice with LARGE gaps. Density of ice < liquid water. When you melt it, the structure collapses, and density increases—unique property.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrogen bonds (partial ionic attraction) are strong compared to other non-covalent forces. They're why water boils at 100°C instead of ~50°C, and why life exists.

image.alt: Hydrogen Bonding & Intermolecular Forces — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Worked Problem: Molecular Geometry & Polarity
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel asks: 'CF₄ and CHF₃ both contain C-F bonds. But one is polar and one isn't. Which, and why?'

example.problem: CF₄ (carbon tetrafluoride) vs CHF₃ (fluoroform): predict shape and polarity.
example.solution: CF₄: C with 4 F. Tetrahedral, symmetric → all dipoles cancel → NONPOLAR. CHF₃: C with 3 F + 1 H. Also tetrahedral, but asymmetric (H less electronegative than F) → dipoles DON'T cancel → POLAR.

slides.inSimpleWords: A molecule's polarity depends on both bond polarity AND shape. Symmetrical molecules can be nonpolar even if bonds are polar.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Molecular Geometry & Polarity — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Your Turn: Design a Molecule
slides.storyContext: Arjun challenges Priya: 'If you want to design a molecule with a strong hydrogen bond, what should you include?'

example.problem: Design a molecule with strong hydrogen bonding. List requirements.
example.solution: Must contain: (1) H bonded to F, O, or N (to create partial positive), (2) F, O, or N with lone pairs to accept the hydrogen bond. Example: ethanol (C₂H₅OH) has O-H group → strong hydrogen bonding. This is why alcohols have high boiling points.

image.alt: Your Turn: Design a Molecule — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Bonding & Structure Essentials

points.text: Ionic: complete electron transfer (high melting point, brittle)
Covalent: electron sharing (variable properties)
Lewis structures show valence electrons; formal charge picks the best structure
Hybridization (sp, sp², sp³) matches bonding geometry
VSEPR predicts shape: electron pairs repel, maximize distance
Hydrogen bonds (H to F/O/N) are strong intermolecular forces—explain water's unique properties

slides.inSimpleWords: Chemical bonds hold atoms together. The type of bond (ionic, covalent, hydrogen bond) and the shape of the molecule determine all its properties.

image.alt: Bonding & Structure Essentials — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

subject: Chemistry
title: Energy & Thermodynamics: Heat, Work & Why Reactions Happen
hook: Why does a candle flame release heat but never needs external energy? Understanding energy changes reveals the why.

slides.title: Thermodynamics
slides.storyContext: Dr. Singh lights a candle in class. 'This flame is just a chemical reaction releasing energy. But what IS energy? Where does it go? Why MUST the reaction happen?'

image.alt: Thermodynamics — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Energy in Chemistry
slides.storyContext: Every reaction moves energy around. Breaking bonds costs energy (endothermic). Forming bonds releases energy (exothermic). The NET change decides if a reaction is spontaneous. This is thermodynamics.

image.alt: Energy in Chemistry — Thermodynamics

slides.title: System, Surroundings, Universe

points.label: System
points.text: The reaction or process we're studying (inside a beaker, inside a cell)

points.label: Surroundings
points.text: Everything else (the room, the air, Earth)

points.label: Universe
points.text: System + Surroundings. Total energy is conserved (First Law).

example.problem: When you burn sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O), identify the system.
example.solution: System = the sugar + oxygen inside the container. Surroundings = the container, room air, everything outside the beaker. The heat released goes TO the surroundings.

slides.inSimpleWords: Think of thermodynamics as energy accounting. The system is what we're studying. The surroundings are everything else. Energy moves between them but is never lost.

image.alt: System, Surroundings, Universe — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Heat, Work & Internal Energy

points.label: Internal Energy (U)
points.text: Total kinetic + potential energy of all particles in the system

points.label: Heat (q)
points.text: Energy transfer due to temperature difference. +q = energy in (endothermic), -q = energy out (exothermic)

points.label: Work (w)
points.text: Energy transfer due to force × distance. Common: PV work when gas expands (w = -PΔV)

example.problem: A gas expands against 1 atm pressure, increasing volume by 2 L. Calculate work.
example.solution: w = -PΔV = -(1 atm)(2 L) = -2 L·atm. Convert: -2 × 101.3 = -202.6 J. Negative = work done BY system ON surroundings.

slides.inSimpleWords: Internal energy is the total energy stored in a substance (heat of atoms moving). Heat is energy transfer due to temperature. Work is energy from pushing against resistance.

image.alt: Heat, Work & Internal Energy — Thermodynamics

slides.title: First Law of Thermodynamics

points.label: Statement
points.text: ΔU = q + w. Change in internal energy = heat + work.

points.label: Conservation
points.text: Energy is never created or destroyed, only transformed.

points.label: Sign convention
points.text: +q: heat absorbed (endothermic), -q: heat released (exothermic), -w: work done by system (expansion)

example.problem: A reaction absorbs 50 J of heat and 20 J of work is done ON the system. Find ΔU.
example.solution: ΔU = q + w = (+50 J) + (+20 J) = +70 J. Internal energy increases by 70 J.

slides.inSimpleWords: The first law says energy is conserved. It can't appear or disappear. A change in internal energy comes from heat and work—nothing else.

image.alt: First Law of Thermodynamics — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Enthalpy & Enthalpy Change

points.label: Enthalpy (H)
points.text: H = U + PV. Useful for reactions at constant pressure (most lab reactions).

points.label: Enthalpy change
points.text: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV). At constant P: ΔH = ΔU + PΔV = q.

points.label: Why ΔH?
points.text: In a lab, we can't easily control internal energy. But we CAN control pressure (use open beakers). ΔH = heat released/absorbed at constant P.

example.problem: Combustion of CH₄: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = -890 kJ. What does this mean?
example.solution: When 1 mole of methane burns at constant pressure, 890 kJ of heat is RELEASED (negative ΔH = exothermic). This heats your home or kitchen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Enthalpy is the 'heat at constant pressure'—exactly what you measure in a lab. Negative ΔH = heat released. Positive ΔH = heat absorbed.

image.alt: Enthalpy & Enthalpy Change — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions

points.label: Exothermic (ΔH < 0)
points.text: Releases heat. Products lower energy than reactants. Examples: combustion, neutralization, respiration.

points.label: Endothermic (ΔH > 0)
points.text: Absorbs heat. Products higher energy than reactants. Examples: melting ice, boiling water, photosynthesis.

points.label: Real-life
points.text: Exothermic reactions are often spontaneous (flame ignites, body burns food). Endothermic reactions need energy input (ice melts only when heated).

example.problem: Melting ice: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l), ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol. Is this spontaneous at room temperature?
example.solution: ΔH > 0 (endothermic). Alone, NO—ice needs heat input. But at T > 0°C, the entropy gain dominates, and ΔG becomes negative (spontaneous). Disorder (liquid) > order (solid) at higher T.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exothermic = heat out (feels warm). Endothermic = heat in (feels cold). Your hand feels cold when ice melts because it's absorbing heat from your skin.

image.alt: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Hess's Law: Adding Reactions

points.label: Principle
points.text: ΔH for a reaction depends only on initial & final states, not path. If you add reactions, add their ΔH values.

points.label: Using Hess's Law
points.text: Break a complex reaction into known simple reactions. Add them algebraically.

points.label: Example
points.text: C(s) + CO₂(g) → 2CO(g). If we know: C + O₂ → CO₂ (ΔH₁), 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ (ΔH₂), we can combine to get the target reaction.

example.problem: Given: (1) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH₁ = -393 kJ. (2) 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g), ΔH₂ = -566 kJ. Find ΔH for: 2C(s) + O₂(g) → 2CO(g).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hess's Law is like adding equations: if you know reaction paths A→B and B→C, you can find ΔH for A→C without running the experiment.

image.alt: Hess's Law: Adding Reactions — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Spontaneity & Gibbs Free Energy (Intro)

points.label: Spontaneous
points.text: Reaction happens on its own without external energy (but may be very slow)

points.label: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS
points.text: Gibbs free energy. ΔG < 0 = spontaneous, ΔG > 0 = non-spontaneous.

points.label: Role of entropy
points.text: ΔS > 0 (disorder increases) favors spontaneity. At high T, TΔS dominates even if ΔH > 0.

example.problem: Melting ice at 0°C: ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol, ΔS = +22 J/(mol·K). Is it spontaneous?
example.solution: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = 6010 J - (273 K)(22 J/K) = 6010 - 6006 ≈ 0. Right at equilibrium. At T > 0°C, TΔS > ΔH, so ΔG < 0 (spontaneous melting).

slides.inSimpleWords: A reaction is spontaneous if ΔG is negative. ΔG weighs enthalpy (energy change) against entropy (disorder change). High temperature favors disorder.

image.alt: Spontaneity & Gibbs Free Energy (Intro) — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Worked Problem: Hess's Law in Practice
slides.storyContext: Dr. Singh assigns a calorimetry lab. Priya must find the heat of formation of NO using Hess's Law.

example.problem: Find ΔH for: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), given: (1) N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂ (ΔH₁ = -68 kJ), (2) 2NO₂ → N₂ + 2O₂ + NO? No, use actual data: (1) 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (ΔH₁ = -114 kJ), (2) N₂ + O₂ → 2NO (ΔH = ?).
example.solution: Given (1): 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, ΔH₁ = -114 kJ. Reverse it: 2NO₂ → 2NO + O₂, ΔH = +114 kJ. Add: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂ (ΔH₂, provided) gives target. Actual ΔH(N₂+O₂→2NO) ≈ +180.5 kJ (endothermic, requires energy—NO is unstable at low T, but high-T engines make it).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hess's Law lets you calculate ΔH for reactions you can't directly measure by combining known reactions.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Hess's Law in Practice — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Why Doesn't Ice Spontaneously Form at Room Temperature?
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Ice melts at 0°C. So at 25°C, shouldn't water spontaneously freeze since that's lower energy?'

example.problem: Freezing water at 25°C: ΔH = -6.01 kJ/mol (releases heat), but ΔS = -22 J/(mol·K) (disorder decreases). Why isn't this spontaneous?
example.solution: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = -6010 - (298 K)(-22 J/K) = -6010 + 6556 = +546 J > 0. Non-spontaneous because the entropy penalty dominates at 298 K. Nature prefers disorder (liquid) over order (ice) at room temperature.

image.alt: Why Doesn't Ice Spontaneously Form at Room Temperature? — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Thermodynamics Essentials

points.text: Internal energy (U) = total energy of particles; changes via heat (q) and work (w)
First Law: ΔU = q + w (energy conserved)
Enthalpy (H): ΔH = heat at constant pressure (lab reactions)
Exothermic: ΔH < 0 (releases heat). Endothermic: ΔH > 0 (absorbs heat)
Hess's Law: ΔH depends on initial & final states, not path
Spontaneity: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. Low ΔG = spontaneous (likely to happen)

slides.inSimpleWords: Thermodynamics explains WHY reactions happen and HOW MUCH energy changes. Energy is conserved. Spontaneous reactions have ΔG < 0, favored by low enthalpy and high entropy.

image.alt: Thermodynamics Essentials — Thermodynamics

subject: Chemistry
title: Balance of Power: Chemical Equilibrium
hook: Why doesn't every reaction go to completion? The answer is equilibrium—a dynamic battle between forward and reverse reactions.

slides.title: Equilibrium
slides.storyContext: Dr. Kumar pours colorless nitrogen dioxide gas into a sealed bottle. Suddenly, it turns brown (N₂O₄). After a while, the color stabilizes. 'It looks done. But it's not. Both reactions are happening, forever.'

image.alt: Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium
slides.storyContext: Most reactions are reversible: A + B ⇌ C + D. At first, forward dominates. Gradually, reverse catches up. When rates match, EQUILIBRIUM is reached—no net change, but both reactions continue. This is dynamic equilibrium.

image.alt: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: Equilibrium Constant (Kc & Kp)

points.label: Definition
points.text: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at constant T: Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b at equilibrium.

points.label: K > 1
points.text: Products favored (equilibrium shifts right)

points.label: K < 1
points.text: Reactants favored (equilibrium shifts left)

points.label: K for gases
points.text: Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations

example.problem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. At equilibrium: [N₂] = 1 M, [H₂] = 3 M, [NH₃] = 2 M. Find Kc.
example.solution: Kc = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³) = (2)² / (1)(3)³ = 4 / 27 ≈ 0.148. K < 1, so reactants (N₂, H₂) are favored; ammonia synthesis is not efficient without pressure/temperature control.

slides.inSimpleWords: The equilibrium constant K measures whether products or reactants are favored. Large K = products win. Small K = reactants win.

image.alt: Equilibrium Constant (Kc & Kp) — Equilibrium

slides.title: Le Chatelier's Principle: Disturbing Equilibrium

points.label: Principle
points.text: When you disturb an equilibrium system, it responds to undo the change.

points.label: Changes
points.text: (1) Concentration: add reactant → shift right (forward). (2) Pressure (gas): increase total P → shift toward fewer moles. (3) Temperature: add heat → shift in endothermic direction.

points.label: Catalyst
points.text: Speeds up both forward & reverse equally → NO shift in equilibrium position.

example.problem: N₂O₄(g, colorless) ⇌ 2NO₂(g, brown). You cool the sealed bottle. Which way does it shift?
example.solution: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is endothermic (takes heat to split). Cooling favors the reverse. Equilibrium shifts LEFT (toward N₂O₄, colorless). Bottle pales.

slides.inSimpleWords: Le Chatelier's Principle: if you stress an equilibrium (add reactant, heat, increase pressure), the system fights back by shifting to oppose the stress.

image.alt: Le Chatelier's Principle: Disturbing Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: Effect of Concentration Changes

points.label: Add reactant
points.text: Equilibrium shifts right (forward) to use up the extra.

points.label: Remove product
points.text: Equilibrium shifts right to make more product.

points.label: Add inert gas at constant V
points.text: No effect (partial pressures of reactants/products unchanged).

points.label: Example: Haber process
points.text: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Industrially, remove NH₃ as it forms (condense it) → forces equilibrium right, improves yield.

example.problem: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. At equilibrium, you inject more H₂. Qualitatively, what happens?
example.solution: Equilibrium shifts RIGHT to consume the extra H₂ and produce more HI. New equilibrium has higher [HI] and [I₂], but [H₂] is restored partially (but still higher than before).

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding more of a reactant pushes the reaction forward. Removing product does the same. This is how industrial chemists maximize output.

image.alt: Effect of Concentration Changes — Equilibrium

slides.title: Effect of Pressure & Volume

points.label: Increasing pressure (decrease volume)
points.text: Shifts equilibrium toward side with FEWER gas moles.

points.label: Example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
points.text: Left: 4 moles (1 N₂ + 3 H₂). Right: 2 moles (2 NH₃). High pressure shifts RIGHT (fewer moles = fewer molecules = lower pressure).

points.label: Industrial
points.text: Haber process runs at ~200-400 atm to shift equilibrium right and maximize NH₃.

example.problem: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). You compress the gas at constant T. Which direction does it shift?
example.solution: Left: 2 moles. Right: 1 mole. High pressure favors fewer moles → shifts RIGHT (forms more N₂O₄). Color fades from brown (NO₂) to colorless (N₂O₄).

slides.inSimpleWords: High pressure favors reactions that produce fewer gas molecules. This is a key strategy in industrial chemistry to boost yields.

image.alt: Effect of Pressure & Volume — Equilibrium

slides.title: Effect of Temperature

points.label: Exothermic reaction (ΔH < 0)
points.text: Heat is a product. Increase T → shifts LEFT (reverse). Decrease T → shifts RIGHT (forward, yields increase).

points.label: Endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0)
points.text: Heat is a reactant. Increase T → shifts RIGHT (forward). Decrease T → shifts LEFT.

points.label: Temperature also changes K
points.text: Pressure/concentration DON'T change K. But T always changes K (changes equilibrium position & magnitude).

example.problem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = -92 kJ (exothermic). For maximum NH₃ yield, should you increase or decrease temperature?
example.solution: Exothermic → heat is a product. Low T shifts equilibrium RIGHT, maximizing NH₃. But low T also slows the reaction (kinetics). Haber uses ~450°C (compromise: acceptable rate + decent yield).

slides.inSimpleWords: For exothermic reactions, cooling pushes equilibrium forward (products). But you lose reaction speed. Industrial chemistry is a balance.

image.alt: Effect of Temperature — Equilibrium

slides.title: Worked Problem: Multi-factor Equilibrium
slides.storyContext: Dr. Kumar assigns a real-world scenario: maximizing acetylene production from calcium carbide (CaC₂ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂).

example.problem: To maximize acetylene yield, should you: (A) increase T, (B) decrease T, (C) remove C₂H₂ as it forms? Assume reaction is exothermic.
example.solution: (B) & (C) are both correct strategies. (B) Low T favors products (exothermic). (C) Removing product forces equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier). Industrially, both are used: water is supplied continuously (removes CaC₂ as it reacts, removes H₂O, shifts forward), and cooling jackets keep T moderate. This drives reaction completion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real industrial chemistry uses multiple Le Chatelier strategies at once: remove products, adjust temperature, optimize pressure—to maximize output.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Multi-factor Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: Ionic Equilibria: Kw & pH

points.label: Water ionization
points.text: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C.

points.label: pH definition
points.text: pH = -log[H⁺]. Neutral: pH 7. Acidic: pH < 7. Basic: pH > 7.

points.label: pOH
points.text: pOH = -log[OH⁻]. pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C.

example.problem: A solution has [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M. Find pH and [OH⁻].

slides.inSimpleWords: Water itself ionizes slightly, creating H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. The product [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ always. pH measures the acidity (H⁺ concentration).

image.alt: Ionic Equilibria: Kw & pH — Equilibrium

slides.title: Design an Industrial Process
slides.storyContext: You're an engineer at a fertilizer plant. You need to maximize ammonia production. What conditions would you recommend?

example.problem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = -92 kJ, K increases with lower T. Recommend: (1) Temperature, (2) Pressure, (3) Concentration management.
example.solution: (1) T: ≈450°C (low enough for good K, high enough for acceptable rate). (2) P: 200-400 atm (shifts toward NH₃, 2 moles < 4 moles). (3) Remove NH₃ as it forms (condense the liquid). This is the Haber process used worldwide—feeding billions.

image.alt: Design an Industrial Process — Equilibrium

slides.title: Equilibrium Mastery

points.text: Equilibrium constant K measures product vs. reactant favorability; depends on T only
Le Chatelier's Principle: system opposes stress (concentration, pressure, T)
Concentration changes: add reactant → shift forward; remove product → shift forward
Pressure (gas): high P → shifts toward fewer moles
Temperature: for exothermic, low T shifts forward; also decreases K
Ionic equilibrium: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴; pH = -log[H⁺]

slides.inSimpleWords: Equilibrium is not 'done'—it's a dynamic balance where forward and reverse reactions continue at the same rate. Le Chatelier's Principle lets you manipulate equilibrium for practical gains.

image.alt: Equilibrium Mastery — Equilibrium

subject: Chemistry
title: Redox Reactions: Electrons Trade Hands
hook: Rusting iron, burning wood, your body using oxygen to extract energy from food—all are redox reactions. Learn the electron trade.

slides.title: Redox Reactions
slides.storyContext: Dr. Rao shows a copper coin turning green in air (oxidation) and asks: 'Why does metal tarnish? What's really happening at the atomic level?'

image.alt: Redox Reactions — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Oxidation & Reduction: A Tale of Electrons
slides.storyContext: Every redox reaction is an electron transfer. One atom LOSES electrons (oxidation), another GAINS (reduction). The atom losing electrons is the reducing agent; the one gaining is the oxidizing agent. Remember: 'OIL RIG' = Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

image.alt: Oxidation & Reduction: A Tale of Electrons — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Oxidation States: Tracking Electrons

points.label: Definition
points.text: Number assigned to an atom reflecting electrons gained/lost. Range: -8 to +8 typically.

points.label: Rules (priority order)
points.text: 1. Element = 0. 2. Monatomic ion = charge. 3. O = -2 (except O₂²⁻ = -1, OF₂ O = +2). 4. H = +1 (except metal hydrides H = -1). 5. Halogens in compounds = -1. 6. Sum of all oxidation states = charge of compound.

example.problem: Find oxidation states in H₂SO₄.
example.solution: H = +1 (rule 4). O = -2 (rule 3). S = ? Sum: 2(+1) + S + 4(-2) = 0 → 2 + S - 8 = 0 → S = +6. (Sulfur in +6 state, even though it has only 6 valence e⁻—it's highly oxidized.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Oxidation states are electron-counting shortcuts. They tell you which atom lost electrons (oxidation state increases) and which gained (oxidation state decreases).

image.alt: Oxidation States: Tracking Electrons — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Identifying Redox Reactions

points.label: Redox?
points.text: Check if any atom's oxidation state CHANGES. If yes → redox.

points.label: Redox type (3 common)
points.text: (1) Combination (synthesis): A + B → AB. (2) Decomposition: AB → A + B. (3) Displacement: AB + C → AC + B.

points.label: Non-redox
points.text: Acid-base (H⁺ transfer), precipitation (ionic rearrangement). Oxidation states don't change.

example.problem: Is this redox? 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
example.solution: Mg: 0 → +2 (oxidation, lost 2 e⁻). O: 0 → -2 (reduction, gained 2 e⁻). YES, this is redox.

slides.inSimpleWords: If oxidation states change, it's a redox reaction. If they don't, it's something else (acid-base, precipitation).

image.alt: Identifying Redox Reactions — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Balancing Redox Equations: Half-Reaction Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Identify oxidation states. Which atom is oxidized? Which reduced?

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Write oxidation half-reaction (loses e⁻) and reduction half-reaction (gains e⁻).

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Balance atoms in each half-reaction (add H₂O, H⁺/OH⁻ as needed for acidic/basic solution).

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Balance electrons (multiply half-reactions so e⁻ gained = e⁻ lost).

points.label: Step 5
points.text: Add half-reactions. Cancel e⁻ and other species.

example.problem: Balance in acidic solution: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺
example.solution: Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Multiply first by 5: 5Fe²⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + 5e⁻. Add: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O (balanced).

slides.inSimpleWords: Split the reaction into what's oxidized and what's reduced. Balance each half separately, then combine. This is the systematic way to handle complex redox.

image.alt: Balancing Redox Equations: Half-Reaction Method — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Oxidizing & Reducing Agents

points.label: Oxidizing agent
points.text: Causes oxidation; itself gets reduced (gains electrons). Example: O₂ (oxygen is oxidizing everything else).

points.label: Reducing agent
points.text: Causes reduction; itself gets oxidized (loses electrons). Example: C (carbon reduces oxygen to CO₂).

points.label: Common agents
points.text: Strong oxidizers: F₂, Cl₂, H₂O₂, KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇. Strong reducers: H₂, C, CO, metals like Zn, Fe.

example.problem: In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, identify the oxidizing and reducing agents.
example.solution: Na: 0 → +1 (oxidized). Cl₂: 0 → -1 (reduced). Na is the REDUCING agent (causes Cl to be reduced). Cl₂ is the OXIDIZING agent (causes Na to be oxidized).

slides.inSimpleWords: The reducing agent is oxidized (loses electrons); the oxidizing agent is reduced (gains electrons). The names describe what they DO, not what happens to them.

image.alt: Oxidizing & Reducing Agents — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Redox in Electrochemistry & Biology

points.label: Electrochemistry
points.text: Galvanic cells: redox reactions generate electrical current (battery). Electrolytic cells: electrical current drives redox reactions (electrolysis).

points.label: Respiration
points.text: Glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy. Glucose is oxidized (loses electrons); O₂ is reduced (gains electrons). Your body extracts energy this way.

points.label: Photosynthesis
points.text: CO₂ + H₂O + light → glucose + O₂. Water is oxidized; CO₂ is reduced. Plants use sunlight to reverse respiration.

example.problem: In respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, identify which is oxidized and reduced.
example.solution: C in glucose: -2 to +4 (in CO₂). Oxidized. O in O₂: 0 → -2 (in H₂O & CO₂). Reduced. The electrons from C flow to O, releasing energy (~2800 kJ/mol)—this powers your cells.

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox reactions power the world: electricity (galvanic cells), your body (respiration), and plants (photosynthesis). Electrons flowing = energy transfer.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Complex Redox Balancing
slides.storyContext: Dr. Rao challenges the class with a reaction from industrial chemistry: dichromate oxidizing ethanol.

example.problem: Balance in acidic solution: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + C₂H₅OH → Cr³⁺ + C₂H₄O (acetaldehyde)
example.solution: C in ethanol: -2 → C in acetaldehyde: -1 (loses 1 e⁻ per C, 2 C total = 2 e⁻ lost). Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻: +6 → Cr³⁺: +3 (gains 3 e⁻ per Cr, 2 Cr = 6 e⁻ gained). Multiply ethanol by 3: 3C₂H₅OH → 3C₂H₄O + 6e⁻. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6e⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Combined: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3C₂H₅OH + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3C₂H₄O + 7H₂O (balanced).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex redox balancing requires careful electron tracking. The half-reaction method handles it systematically—split, balance, multiply, combine.

slides.title: Types of Redox Reactions

points.label: Combination (synthesis)
points.text: 2C + O₂ → 2CO. Both reactants change oxidation state.

points.label: Decomposition
points.text: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. Single compound breaks; products have different oxidation states.

points.label: Displacement
points.text: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. More reactive metal displaces less reactive from its salt.

points.label: Disproportionation
points.text: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO. Same element oxidized AND reduced in one reaction. Cl: 0 → -1 (in HCl, reduced) and 0 → +1 (in HClO, oxidized).

example.problem: Is Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O a disproportionation?
example.solution: Cl in Cl₂: 0. Cl in NaCl: -1 (reduced). Cl in NaClO: +1 (oxidized). YES, disproportionation. Same Cl atom family gains and loses electrons simultaneously.

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox reactions come in patterns. Disproportionation is tricky—one atom is oxidized and reduced at the same time (like Cl in bleach production).

slides.title: Redox in Your Life: Rust & Corrosion
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees rust on a bicycle and asks: 'Why does iron rust, and how can we stop it?'

example.problem: Iron rusting: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2H₂O → 4FeO·OH (rust). Identify oxidation states & the redox process.
example.solution: Fe: 0 → +3 (oxidized, loses 3e⁻ per Fe). O: 0 → -2 (reduced, gains 2e⁻ per O). This is a redox reaction. Prevention: paint (blocks O₂), galvanizing (coat with Zn, which oxidizes first), alloys (stainless steel, Cr prevents oxidation).

slides.title: Redox Reactions Summary

points.text: Oxidation = loss of electrons (oxidation state increases)
Reduction = gain of electrons (oxidation state decreases)
Redox reactions involve electron transfer between atoms
Oxidation states track electrons; sum to compound charge
Half-reaction method: split into oxidation & reduction, balance, multiply, combine
Oxidizing agent is reduced; reducing agent is oxidized
Redox powers batteries, respiration, and industry

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox is electron transfer. Atoms that lose electrons are oxidized; those that gain are reduced. Mastering redox balancing (half-reaction method) is key to Class 11 chemistry.
